records.title: Show HN: I told people I'm a convicted felon after 20 years of hiding it
records.author: buf
records.storyText:
Hi there.

I was engineer number 3 at Eventbrite and founding engineer at Reforge. I've created a dozen or so startups myself and have worked in many others, like Instacart. All this time, no one knew that I was a convicted felon.

It wasn't exactly a topic that came up, but it was certainly something that I never brought up. When you're a convicted felon, people look at you as if you are tainted.

I was unable to rent apartments in San Francisco. I was unable to get a job directly after being released from prison. It's funny because when you owe the state $17,000 in restitution and you can't get a job, people become extremely desperate. And that desperation can easily put you right back into prison.

So I went from homeless person at age 19 to 7-figures about 10 years later. I retired at age 38.

What I'm doing now is writing an autobiography. The main theme of it is hope.

And I want to make sure that people know about it. They don't necessarily have to be interested in it, but if people know about what it's like sleeping in a car believing that one day you will travel the world and then actually doing it, then I think I've accomplished my task in writing this book.

If you're interested, please let me know.

records.title: Show HN: Gauge CLI – Open-Source Hillclimbing for Agent Experience
records.author: 0x63_Problems
records.storyText:
Hi HN! We're releasing an open-source CLI for hillclimbing Agent Experience. That means optimizing your agent-facing surfaces (Skills, CLIs, SDKs, and docs) so that your users' coding agents can easily use your product. Pointing your own agent at the repo is enough to get started. https://github.com/gauge-sh/gauge-cli

We've found that power users generally want to hand a CLI/MCP to their agents and get started from the terminal. They rarely want to log in and use the web UI themselves. We think developer tools must be agent-friendly to remain relevant.

Here are some common findings that Gauge identifies:

- agents get confused with CLI/SDK behavior and start source diving - interactive commands block agents - agents use deprecated/old CLI commands - agents don't use Skills when you'd expect - agents confidently assert limitations that don't exist - inconsistent terminology confuses agents - agents can't figure out how commands fit together into a workflow

Locally, the Gauge CLI uses Docker containers to run agent harnesses (you can bring your own subscriptions). It finds where agents get confused or stuck and tests changes using your pre-release artifacts (Skills/CLI etc). We normalize events from Claude Code, Codex, Pi and OpenCode into standardized transcripts, and store them locally, alongside structured information in SQLite so that your agent can easily analyze the data. This enables automatic hillclimbing toward a great Agent Experience.

We also offer hosted compute that enables more features, built on our custom Gateway (for credential brokering and transparent, per-session response rewriting). Hosted compute enables many more concurrent sessions, easier collaboration with teammates, a GitHub App for PR reviews, sessions with logged-in MCPs/APIs, and most importantly it lets you close your laptop while the sessions actually run.

You don't need a Gauge account to run the full loop end-to-end though. We expect that local execution with the CLI is enough to find and fix several agent experience issues in a typical project.

You'll be able to validate fixes for these issues locally, before publishing new versions (we inject pre-release Skills and code artifacts into the sessions).

We would love your feedback!

records.title: Show HN: Jev drives a browser – HN login and search in 8s for half a cent
records.author: zurfyx
records.storyText:
I put this repo and site together as an educational reference for folks getting started with Jev / OpenAI Decisions API.

This demonstrates how Jev can drive a browser (the idea being extract it into a skills file). On every step the page's controls are extracted into a table, and Jev picks an operation and a target, with a probability for every option.

Try the HN login replay (https://jev-browser.rovira.sh/#hackernews-login), Amazon (https://jev-browser.rovira.sh/#amazon-cart), or run it live with your own key.

Interesting bits: - Jev mean response time is 250ms (123–495 ms on the HN run). - Jev never sees the DOM, only a table of controls extracted from it ahead of time. It's in some ways, similar to the accessibility tree that good LLM browser skills use now. - Jev can't generate text (in a good way) so this need to be provided ahead of time, either by you or a complementary LLM. - Each step is stateless and costs a few thousand input tokens, under a tenth of a cent.

Repo (three files, no dependencies): https://github.com/zurfyx/jev-browser-skill

records.title: Show HN: TUI to manage firewall and HTTP server, in Rust
records.author: FabCH
records.storyText:
I have been self-hosting for 10 years, and "family hosting" for 2.

The number of attacks my servers get has increased by 3x since May of this year. Now personally, I don't like hiding behind Cloudflare because I don't want them to be a SPOF, but it was becoming a bit too scary to just be open to the web. Because it is a family cloud, it can't hide behind a VPN, it has to support devices like TV sticks that can't connect properly over VPN. It has to support HTTPS.

So I put together a Rust/Ratatui TUI+cron/CLI that manages my second line of defense: firewall and HTTP server. I run a reverse Nginx proxy in front of apps like Nextcloud, and a nftables firewall with SSH as my admin tunnel. It does several things:

1) It allows me to block entire segments, countries, datacenter IP ranges, TOR exit nodes etc...

2) It allows me to block specific bots: search bots, AI bots, security scanners

3) It does dynamic blocking too, looking at the logs to spot bad behavior and block it. I used to run fail2ban for SSH for example, but a centralized UI for both SSH and HTTP(S) is nicer IMHO.

So if this is useful to anyone else, feel free. It's AGPL v3.

In my experience, geoblocking is the biggest win, reducing the attacks by 30x.

AI Disclosure: I use AI assisted development. I follow Linus Torvalds and Bob Martin model, with using AI as a tool and verifying the result.

records.author: nomemory
records.storyText:
I am avid reader of blogs (always been since 2005 onwards), so it was always on my list to build a rss reader at some point.

Initially I've built lectura for myself (the first version started when I've experimented with server side rendering/Thymeleaf + Spring Boot) and self hosted on a server (without a domain). Then I decided to vibecode multi user support. And this is the final result.

What are some highlights:

- It doesn't track/record what the users are doing. There are no emails (no password recovering in case you lose your password). The only information that's kept are your own subscription, that others can see as well. But that's it. Because of this, creating a username takes 5 seconds (depending on how fast you write);

- It supports different layouts that I find useful with my RSS reader. For example there's a 'random' content view so you can read "historical articles" you've might missed. There's a another view called 'Quiet Sources' so you can 'prioritise' blogs that don't publish often. I'll let you find the other views.

- It has good accesibility support, or it should. If not, drop me some feedback;

- For the moment it's free. I don't expect a big influx of users (who uses a RSS reader + reading blogs nowadays) so I have a cheap dedicated server at 20$ per month. With the current resources, unless someone really wants to "put it down", it should work with a few hundred users (reading concurrently). I can afford paying 20$ montly withouthing thinking to ask for money, at least for the moment.

That's it.

I don't have experience with 'products', 'startups', etc. This is just a project I hope will be useful to someone other than me. If not, i will keep using it as my "premium" RSS reader :).

Cheers, Andrei

records.title: Show HN: Koody for Business – AI bookkeeping for people who aren't accountants
records.author: Halimah
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Hallie, founder of Koody. Today, I'm launching Koody for Business: AI-powered accounting, bookkeeping, and tax prep software for sole proprietors and small businesses.

For years, I used accounting software for my business. I went into it to create invoices, categorize and reconcile transactions, and work with my accountant to prepare our books. I often dreaded having to do it. There were so many transactions to get through in a handful of different currencies, and I found the whole process draining.

The software I used (and refuse to name) worked really well. It was capable accounting software, and I'm not trying to suggest otherwise. But for me, accounting had become a bit like going to the dentist. You know it's necessary and useful, but that doesn't stop you from feeling anxious about it or wishing you didn't have to go.

What makes this personal is that I've always been good at accounting. Throughout secondary school, I was the best student in every financial accounting class. I was also the class prefect, so I would regularly collect everyone's homework and take it to the staff room for submission. My accounting teacher used to ask me to put mine on top because she used it as a marking guide.

I then went on to study finance in undergrad and eventually earned an MBA. So accounting isn't an unfamiliar subject to me, yet dealing with my own books made me extremely sad and anxious.

I'm building Koody for Business because I want business owners to see accounting through my original lens: something simple and enjoyable that doesn't require a degree to understand.

Koody automatically categorizes business income and expenses and uses those transactions to produce cash flow insights, profit and loss reports, and records for Schedule C and tax prep.

There are two workspaces: personal and business. The business workspace lets you manage your business finances separately from your personal finances, even when you use the same bank account for both, as many sole proprietors do. You can keep each transaction in the appropriate workspace, so personal spending stays out of your business reports. You can use Koody just for your business, just for your personal finances, or for both.

Give Koody for Business a try at koody.com/business. I'd love to hear what you think.

About two years ago, I built KeyboardStack as my first macOS app. Since then, I've kept working on it, fixing bugs, improving things, and adding new features.

I spend a lot of time in front of my computer, and I'm always looking for ways to be more productive. Constantly switching between my keyboard and mouse or trackpad was slowing me down and breaking my flow, even for something as simple as clicking a button.

I wanted to be able to navigate my entire Mac using just my keyboard, across all my apps.

So I built KeyboardStack, a native macOS app that lets you navigate, click, and scroll without having to reach for your mouse or trackpad.

One feature is the Grid Mode. Press ⌃H to display a grid on your screen, type a few letters, and click anywhere. There are also other modes for navigating clickable elements, scrolling, and moving the cursor.

There are already some great apps like Homerow. What I wanted to do differently was combine keyboard hints with a grid, so you can still click anywhere, even when an element isn't detected as clickable.

Grid Mode is completely free and will stay free forever. The other modes are available for a $29.99 one-time purchase. No subscription.

Website: https://keyboardstack.com

I'm still working on KeyboardStack and would love to hear what you think. Any feedback, bug reports, or feature suggestions are welcome! I'm also happy to answer any questions about how it works.

records.title: Show HN: KeibiDrop – Work on remote large files on-demand (no upload/download)
records.author: coldstartops
records.storyText:
We have built KeibiDrop because me and the people close to me were tired of cloud storages, and to copy data fully across our devices in order to use it.

Now with KeibiDrop you can mount and stream folders between your computers (and web browser) access and edit data on-demand as if it was local.

You can try it instantly in the browser https://web.keibidrop.com/ (you need two devices) or by building from source/ downloading from the github releases. (there are also demo recordings in the Readme on github).

We also got a marketing website for it here: https://keibidrop.com

The desktop app, engine and CLI are FOSS AGPL-v3 and in terms of architecture and stack the following holds:

- It uses a full-duplex P2P IPv6 connection between peers with a fallback to a data forwarding relay.

- We got a dual networking stack QUIC + TCP using protocol buffers (WebRTC to be added), and we use ML-KEM-1024 + X25519 for the handshake and either aes-gcm-256 or chacha20-poly1305 for the session, and we do a latency hiding re-key inspired by Signal's SPQR.

- it relies on FUSE, macFUSE, and WinFsp as filesystem drivers and the whole gist of it is to "hide the latency" of remote filesystems and to just give the feeling of teleporting files.

- we use golang for the engine, and rust + slint.dev for the GUI

Our goal was to have a lightweight, cross platform filesystem that does not use many resources, has the RAM usage bounded and gives the feeling as if working on a local filesystem.

Currently the filesystem respects POSIX semantics, (except for symlinks and hardlinks, I have them disabled), and we tested it on intercontinental links (between Romania and Singapore), on both relayed connections and direct connections.

You can use git, pijul, Premiere Pro, DaVinci Resolve or any tools you would normally use on your local computer, or use our docker image on your NAS storage and instantly access the data you need while you are travelling.

records.title: Show HN: Daily Pipes: A daily tile-rotation puzzle that never requires guessing
records.author: jkelle
records.storyText:
This is my first game that actually shipped!

I built this because I like making games, but I always get bogged down in feature creep or making the art look good. I constrained myself with this project to a simple game with little to no bells and whistles and an emphasis on shipping.

The core puzzle itself isn't my original idea. It's a classic puzzle you can find on other sites, and it has several variations. My goal was to turn it into a daily puzzle with some nice features on top like stats and a share mechanic.

The Algorithm: I generate boards offline by building a random spanning tree and then scrambling it. Then I check if the resulting scrambled board has exactly one solution solution and can be solved without needing to guess-and-backtrack. If so, it goes into the puzzle bank, otherwise I reject it.

I compute a difficulty score for each kept board using the heuristic of "longest chain of deductions" needed to solve it. I originally tried estimating difficulty from how many turns the scramble took, but that turned out not to capture difficulty very well at all.

The daily puzzles ramp up in difficulty throughout the week, with Monday being the easiest and Sunday the hardest.

The Stack: It's a static Vite/TypeScript site on Cloudflare Pages and sends basic usage metrics to PostHog.

I chose to keep all the player data in the browser's local storage because keeping the server stateless helped the whole project stay lightweight.

I'm a more of a backend dev and sometimes data scientist at my day job, so the web stack was new to me. This was my first time using Cloudflare directly, and I didn't even know about PostHog before.

Claude implemented almost all the code, but if feel like I still learned conceptually how these components work and fit together.

Play: There are no sign-ups, accounts, or downloads. Free to play. No ads. Just a simple web game.

My most recent addition is a stats page with a couple bar charts and a GitHub-style activity tracker.

The archive feature is "coming soon". It's an example of a feature I punted on so I can ship sooner. I'm measuring demand before implementing it by allowing users to enter their email and saying it'll be $5. TBD if I actually charge for it.

Feel free to play and share it with those in your life who enjoy daily puzzle games!

Would love to get any feedback.

records.title: Show HN: Frink – Desktop-first app for multi-step workflows and parallel agents
records.author: norvalbv
records.storyText:
What’s up HN?! I'm Benji, and I’ve been building Frink since ~April this year.

Frink is a desktop-first, open-source (MIT) app for running coding agents in parallel and multi-step workflows that start on their own. It runs on your machine (macOS and Linux) with your own provider login. It currently supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot, and OpenCode, but the latter 3 are in preview. No Frink account to use the app.

The biggest USP of Frink is workflows: think n8n for agents. You describe a routine in a sentence, for example: "every weekday at 9am, run the tests; if any fail, have an agent fix them, then wait for my approval before it opens a PR." Then, Frink builds it as a workflow (or simply, Flow): a list of steps you can read and change before it runs. A Flow can start on a schedule, from any webhook, or from an event from a third-party such as Linear, Shortcut, ClickUp, Sentry, PostHog, etc. Steps can be agent turns, shell commands, conditions, approval steps that stop and wait for you, or steps you write yourself in code (or ask the agent to write one). Everything that needs you (an approval, an agent's question, a finished task to review) lands in one Work Queue.

Other stuff:

* Up to four agents side by side, each on its own git worktree if you want. Or, many agents out of direct view.

* Every change shows as a diff; there's a code editor, a terminal, etc.

* Local-first: chats, Flows and tasks live in SQLite on your machine.

* Easier provider parity: currently working on and improving the tooling setup between providers. Once inside Frink, irrespective of what provider you use, the hooks, MCPs, and other tooling work out of the box between providers.

Why I built it: I started building it when there weren’t many other competitors; now the industry is swamped with ADEs and harnesses. However, in my opinion, each still lacks good automation for more fine-tuned scenarios. I doubled down on the flows to help me with my actual day-to-day job as a SWE, and over time it’s helped me automate most of the PRs being shipped across my personal projects, team, etc., to the point that it’s a continuous loop and helps a whole ton.

Notes: Windows isn't supported yet. Flows only run on Claude Code and Codex for now. It's a solo project, so expect sharp edges.

records.title: Show HN: New Forms of Reading
records.author: John_1-1
records.storyText:
In an effort to develop new forms of reading, I’ve built a minimalistic Bible app (only on iOS for now), called John 1:1. The Bible is well-suited because it: (i) has a history of driving reading innovations and revolutions (e.g., 2nd century: scroll -> codex; Gutenberg in Mainz, 1454: codex -> movable metal type; Estienne in Geneva, 1551: introduction of verse numbers); (ii) remains popular and widespread, with public domain translations in many languages (the app ships ten translations in seven languages); and (iii) is intrinsically self-linking and annotated over millennia (31,102 verses; +500,000 cross-references). Few texts have such a dense pre-existing edge list.

John 1:1 tries to extend the Bible’s arc of reading innovations to and through the mobile device by organizing verses in a swipe feed that can be navigated vertically and horizontally. Navigating via these two axes enables two distinct forms of reading: linear and lateral. To read linearly (Genesis 1:1 -> Genesis 1:2) a user swipes up, and the next verse appears below. To read laterally, means to read verses that are connected or related, but not next to each other. Swipe left from Genesis 1:2 (“formless and void, and darkness was over the surface of the deep”) and Jeremiah 4:23 appears from the right, with that same, rare language (“I looked at the earth, and it was formless and void”). That swipe (Genesis 1:2 -> Jeremiah 4:23) crosses +19,000 verses or ~ 61% of the Bible. One could read the Bible linearly for decades and never realize that Jeremiah 4:23 echoes Genesis 1:2. Lateral reading can therefore reveal a hidden structure, and meaning, that cannot be detected through linear reading. The app ships with 292,374 lateral connections. The key challenge has been how best to score “a human will see why these two things are related” at build time. If anybody knows or has a good idea, please tell me!

John 1:1 is free (no ads, no accounts, no in-app purchases, fully offline) and there are no plans to monetize it. However, lateral reading can be applied to any text with addressable units, a pre-existing edge list, connection logic, and ranking. And there are many promising applications in law, academia, or any other domain in which humans will continue to closely read complex texts and benefit from a tool that makes hidden information visible.

records.title: Show HN: Euspell – Spelling reform: an enginnering approach
records.author: kamranossia
records.storyText:
Hi HN. Euspell is a conservastive respelling of English and all the software needed to implement it. The link above converts the text you paste, in your browser. Other ways to try it out are the browser extensions and EPUB/PDF readers.

Previous spelling reforms have failed for two reasons: they asked people to apply rules by hand or remember a large set of new spellings, and they couldn't handle homographs: "read" is reed or red, "records" is a noun or a verb, "wound" is an injury or a past tense - writing in pure phonetics will actually create hundreds of homographs. Euspell approaches spelling reform differently, with the goal of aiding reading and comprehension.

- A lexicon with 205505 entries, each with CLAWS7 part-of-speech tags. Of these, 164067 (80%) are left unchanged. No diacritics are used. Proper nouns are untouched. American spelling is the base, in the line of Webster's reforms. - 5920 entries are ambiguous and need context. The noun/verb -s split (records/recordz) is a linear SVM: 93.2% on held-out text. The hand-written rule it replaced scored 75.9%. The full evaluation is at https://github.com/ossiak/euspell/blob/main/docs/paper-evalu... - Semantic splits (e.g. bow, tear, lead) are hand-written rules and less accurate: "read" gets about four in five right on its test set. - Runs locally in a browser extension (Chrome/Firefox/Safari, including PDFs), MS Word, LibreOffice, Google Docs, and a standalone EPUB/PDF reader for Windows, MacOS, Android and iOS. - Code is GPL-3.0, lexicon is CC BY-SA 4.0: https://github.com/ossiak/euspell. White paper: https://euspell.org/paper

The changes can be toggled on and off: Euspell changes what you read, not the source text. AI tools (Claude) helped with the software, the site and the videos; the reform and the lexicon are mine. There is also a 14-part video series: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLfCd5hTV7IWg

Most useful feedback: sentences where it picks the wrong spelling.

records.title: Show HN: Peras – Pause Claude Code and Codex before they burn your weekly limit
records.author: vertias3u
records.storyText:
Hello HN! Today I am presenting you with Peras, the tool which governs your Claude Code and Codex usage, and enforces limits. I built it because I got tired of constantly having to spam /usage to check my usage, and decide if a task is worth risking the agent running out mid-task.

Peras enforces a limit with 2 main tiers. At 75% weekly usage you will get a notification, and at 90% Peras will automatically pause the agent. These limits are the default and they are customizable to your own liking.

You may ask "how does it know my usage in Claude Code or Codex?" Well, it's pretty simple. Peras gets the Claude Code usage % from the status line, and Codex's one comes from its local app-server. The "pause" Peras executes is a hook that refuses the agent's tool calls and ends its turn.

A new feature I implemented is one that makes agents aware of their own usage. When you send your prompt, Peras attaches the usage %. It sends it at the start of the session, then again at 50, 75, 90 and 100%, or if a reset is coming in 30 minutes, so the agent can hurry up and actually capitalize on the remaining usage, if any. Just to clarify, this feature is informational and the pause is what enforces the limit.

Before I switched to native SwiftUI, I used SwiftBar. The problem was that for the mascots patrolling their usage bars, I had to re-encode every menu image 8 times a second! There was also stuff SwiftBar wasn't capable of, like the menu being able to appear over fullscreen apps, pinning it as a floating panel, etc.

What is the difference between the free and paid version? Well, it is MIT, first of all. The CLI, the hooks, the SwiftBar menu, and the app's source are all on GitHub, but building the app needs macOS 13+, Node 18+, "xcode-select --install" and then finally "npm run build:app". The €4.99 buys you a signed copy which is notarized by Apple, with updates included. The guard works with no menu at all. To install, just run:

  npx peras-cli setup
  npx peras-cli codex setup
And now we get to the limits part. For now it's subscription plans only, and when running "claude -p", the pause uses the last interactive reading, so it can come late. Also I feel I have to mention that the guard rail is not a security boundary. It runs inside the agent. The menu is macOS only. The CLI and hooks pass tests on Linux in CI, but I don't use them there day-to-day.

Last thing before I end this post, I would really appreciate feedback from you, whether install worked for Codex users, whether you have encountered any bugs, or whatever you feel like sharing.

records.title: Show HN: Photonica – Film looks for your photos, processed locally with WebGPU
records.author: topvlad
records.storyText:
Photonica is a browser editor that processes your photos without server uploading or registration.

I'm Vlad, an engineering lead and a hobby mobile photographer. I like film aesthetics but don't like carrying a film camera with me. It all started with film emulation experiments on the server with heavy processing and evolved into a more convenient web app. I want to help everyone (including myself) to quickly get a film look, because I think each photo has its own vibe, so one preset just can't fit them all.

The app can apply baked LUTs from spectral film models (spektrafilm by Andrea Volpato and Spectral Film LUT by Jan Lohse) and gives you a variety of tools for making artistic photos. I added tools to work with halation, diffusion, grain, a print stage with paper exposure, and Space - a two-pad color grade.

Free version gives you: set of films on all nine print papers, 3 exports a day without an account (unlimited with a free account). Pro is $2.99/month, $19.99/year or $49 once: more films, optics and light effects, collages with instagram carousel slides, original-resolution export. All spektrafilm LUTs are free.

There's only a web version (no native apps), but you can install it as a PWA (to use it on your phones). The only requirement is WebGPU support (JPEG/HEIC, no RAW support yet).

I hope this tool will help you too to make more beautiful images. I would appreciate any feedback about how the app works on your device and whether it's easy to get film look from "phone photos".

Examples and before/after: https://photonica.studio

records.title: Show HN: SchemaWright, learning database design in a gamified way
records.author: devgabrielmarco
records.storyText:
Let me begin by explaining what it is: SchemaWright is a platform for learning database table design in a gamified way, with a real Postgres database running on your browser via WASM. It was heavily inspired by Duolingo and LeetCode, because I love the way how those platforms teach their users.

I built and launched this a couple months ago, weeks after my first SaaS failed (that one was called NoteRaven, and the idea was for it to be a Notion + Medium + Udemy all in one platform; but after looking at how saturated that market was, I decided to move on).

The story on how I came up with it is basically that I was working normally on my day job, and noticed how many times we had changed some core tables, and usually discussed renaming them, changing columns, relationships etc. After that, I realized that I wanted to learn how to "get the schema right" from the beginning, so I began looking for websites that could teach that.

It didnt take long to realize I couldn't find one that fitted my needs: it had to feel gamified and rigorous at the same time. When I say "rigorous" I mean that the content shouldnt be standard exercises we see in university (that we never really use at work) or loose definitions we feel like is too shallow. Therefore, I decided that I would be the one to build such platform.

The way I structured the app is by separating it in 3 main pages: Learn, Exercises and Lectures.

The first one is where you'll find Duolingo like lessons for database schema, it goes from the foundations (what is a table, what are rows and columns), to intermediate/advanced contents, such as concurrency and queues, scaling and architecture etc. It has 8 levels, but I currently only wrote up to level 3 (normalisation). Which is funny because my boss once tested me on this lol.

The Exercises page is where I took inspiratoin from LeetCode, especially the page for an exercise structure: on the left side you have the problem description, your submissions and an editorial, and on the right side the code editor and the tests that will run on your code.

Finally the last page is for people who are keen on reading papers and are more drawn to academic research. The lectures reference famous and important research papers that led us to our current understanding of databases, sql and concepts we learn today on this subject. It summarizes them and teaches you the concepts, while containing some interactive exercises too!

Ok, so why do I think this may work as opposed to NoteRaven? One of the reasons is that I shared this with my co-workers (60+ people, most are devs too) and boss (who is CEO and CTO), and they really enjoyed using it. That same boss gave me positive feedback and suggestions, that I actually ended up implementing on the platform (yeah your suggestion could end up there too!). Another would be that I feel like platforms that train you on database design are scarce compared to ones that teach you queries, so the market wouldn't be so saturated.

Let me know what you guys think! Please share if you think some exercises are unfair, meaning that they need better context for people to answer them, and also what you think of the lesson's pace, content and interactive exercises; the same goes for the lectures.

records.title: Show HN: Daily password puzzle game with real passwords from data breaches
records.author: walker1993
records.storyText:
I created this online puzzle game where one daily real password from data breaches has to be guessed in Wordle-style. Once you solve it, you see how many accounts actually used that password (Source: Have I Been Pwned). It's free, needs no sign-up, and takes a minute.

I work in digital forensics and I come across passwords every day, and the patterns are always the same ones. Daily Crack started above all as a small awareness campaign on this topic. You might find your own password and discover it's used by hundreds of thousands of other people. Or realise that six attempts are enough to guess a complete stranger's password, because it follows the same pattern as yours.

I’d love feedback on difficulty: are six attempts too many?

records.title: Show HN: iOS location based traveler's currency conversion with tax estimations
records.author: rock_artist
records.storyText:
I've made this app a while ago and now updated it with responsive UI and nice widgets.

Why did I make it?

During my travels to the US and Canada, I wanted to see prices in my currency. however, in both countries, prices are shown BEFORE tax. which adds more confusion.

This conversion apps uses location and locale to try and automatically provide estimations closer to what you'll pay based on your location. It's limited (since tax differs between products) but it's good enough to get a better estimation.

It also includes nice overview of tipping customs (I do hope to make this into an open wiki based if enough demand exists), and Tax Free information.

While I do hope to introduce Android release, It's written in SwiftUI and benefits from Apple's frameworks. so it targets iDevices (iPhone, iPads/Apple Silicon and Apple Watch)

records.title: Show HN: Open-source edge data governance library
records.author: djekershaw
records.storyText:
CsvPath Framework is a Python data firewall that protects downstream systems from bad data getting past the ingress point. Data is much easier to fix when you shift quality control left, remove manual data checking, stop accumulating orphaned ingestion code, and decrease the skills consumed by data pipelines.

The Framework:

- registers inbound data into an immutable, versioned staging area, with a cryptographic identity,

- validates and upgrades it using one or more of five validation languages,

- generates ops and lineage metadata for OpenLineage and OpenTelemetry,

- and publishes results data and metadata to a versioned immutable archive with no-code integrations downstream.

CsvPath Framework refers to these bullets as "data preboarding".

Supports: JSON Schema, ODCS, XSD, XPath, and CsvPath Validation Language (CVL) validation. Ingests: JSON, JSONL, XML, CSV, Excel, Pandas DataFrames, live Python objects. Backends: AWS, Azure, GCP, SFTP, local; also FlightPath Server

Website: https://www.csvpath.org

records.title: Show HN: dp_intl – Gettext-compatible internationalization library for C++
records.author: danpla
records.storyText:
dp_intl is intended to be an enhanced version of the Gettext runtime library (also known as libintl), with the following improvements:

* dp_intl does not depend on the locale. In contrast, Gettext requires the use of the setlocale() function from the C standard library, which alters the behavior of other locale-dependent C routines, leading to subtle bugs that only arise in specific locales. For example, a floating-point number serialized by snprintf() with a locale that uses a period as a decimal separator will not be parsed correctly by strtof() with a locale that uses a comma, and vice versa. Another example is tolower() and strcasecmp(), which will break with the Turkish locale, where the lowercase of "I" is "ı" rather than "i".

* dp_intl uses 64-bit integers for plural form routines on all platforms. In contrast, Gettext routines (e.g. ngettext()) use the unsigned long type, making it impossible to write cross-platform code without limiting your numbers to 2³² (4,294,967,295). Otherwise, translations for numbers greater than 2³² will have incorrect plural forms due to unsigned wrap around (modulo 2³²) on systems with a 32-bit unsigned long (e.g., 64-bit Windows).

* Unlike Gettext, dp_intl is not tied to local file system: it reads files through a virtual stream class that can wrap any file-like object, including those from archives and packages (like an APK on Android).

* dp_intl allows any language in source strings. In contrast, the Gettext routines for translating plural form messages (e.g., ngettext()) are limited to English and several other languages with two plural forms: "one" for 1 and "many" for all other numbers, making it impossible to use any other language that doesn't fit this pattern.

records.title: Show HN: My attempt to get Claude to run a business
records.author: diegoaad
records.storyText:
On Sunday, I decide to give it a try and asked Claude to come up with a business idea and run it.

I installed it in an Ubuntu VPS, setup some accounts like Stripe, Cloudflare and let it decide on the idea, stack, promotion, etc.

It created this app: https://pagecritic.app/ that let people evaluate their landing page and scores it on 7 different items, evaluating things like clarify, value prop, CTA and so on.

You can try it for free and get a reduced report, or pay for a full report (first few HN users would be able to get full report for free as well).

The idea was interesting, it was able to build it pretty fast and get it up and running.

I had to help with some account setup, but it basically tried in different ways to launch/promote the app, but distribution is definitely a problem for agent run business.

It can do decent job on get it up and running and react to failures, but in my opinion is not really able to promote the business by itself.

I gave it a channel to Telegram, so it can always ask me for things on Telegram and it did ask for money to pay for advertising it in some launch boards. But still it's not able to really drive much traffic.

The nice thing it did was to make the whole journey public, so you can see it's journal: https://pagecritic.app/journal and some live numbers: https://pagecritic.app/stats

For folks who did similar experiment, has anyone been able to get some substantial revenue out of it? Or this only works if you're an influencer with thousands of followers?

records.title: Show HN: Honu – builds microapps that float on your Mac desktop
records.author: ctchuang
records.storyText:
Honu is a small macOS app. A turtle sits on your desktop; you tell it what you want (“a world clock”, “a habit tracker”) and Claude Code writes a tiny app that pops out as a floating bubble. To change an app, type what you want into the bar below the bubble and every running microapps get updated altogether (ex: ask it to “change color to blue”). To delete one, drag it to the octopus emerging from the screen bottom.

Under the hood it invokes `claude -p` for each request, so it runs on your existing Claude account with no API key. Model choice is fixed to Opus 5.5.

If you already have Claude Code, the quickest start is to run claude in the repo and ask it to “run it”. It does not require Xcode.

Caveats: it’s a very early experimental prototype, and there’s no protection against prompt injection, so treat it as a toy.

The first version was Rust+egui, but I couldn’t get webview embedded properly, so I asked Claude Code in one sentence to rewrite the whole 3,000 lines in Swift, and it did! So far it’s fun but maybe not very useful. It feels magic to see the microapps changing look instantly after you type in new ideas under the bubble.
